subtitle: Fraction forms of rational numbers, roots and pi, and placing an irrational number on the number line

problems.desc: (c) rubric for the marked number line: the dot must sit between the seventh and eighth whole-number ticks, visibly past the midpoint of that interval (the value is about seven and one third), and it must be labelled with the square root symbol or the rounded decimal. A dot placed left of the midpoint, or on a tick, does not earn credit.

Rubric for the shown work: the derivation must set the repeating decimal equal to a variable, multiply by ten, subtract the original equation so the repeating tails cancel, and reach a whole-number right-hand side before dividing. Credit the argument only when the subtraction step is written out; a bare correct fraction with no shown cancellation does not show that the decimal is rational.

(b) rubric: the written reason must connect the computed whole-number value to the definition of rational, i.e. the root came out a whole number and every whole number can be written over one, so the number is a ratio of two integers. An answer that only repeats the value, or that says the root sign makes it irrational, earns no credit.

(b) rubric for the marked number line: two labelled dots, both between the ticks at three and one tenth and three and two tenths, with the dot for the ratio twenty-two sevenths placed to the RIGHT of the dot for the circle constant. Credit requires the correct left-right order, not exact placement.

(b) rubric: the answer must say that Tomas confused 'never ends' with 'never repeats'. A decimal that eventually repeats a fixed block forever is rational, and part (a) produced the fraction that proves it; only a decimal that never ends AND never settles into a repeating block is irrational. Naming the repeating block, or citing the fraction found in part (a), is required for full credit.
